seoTitle: Create a Landing Page in Power BI Dashboards
metaDescription: Build a landing page for a Power BI report: a title, a placeholder visual, and Power BI's built-in page navigator, plus how its page visibility settings really work.
intro:
The first page of a Power BI dashboard sets the tone for how stakeholders engage with your data, and it's the one page almost everyone sees whether they explore further or not. Instead of dropping viewers straight into a dense, chart-filled report the moment it opens, a dedicated landing page gives them a title, a sense of what's inside, and clear navigation to the pages that matter to them. That matters most for reports shared broadly across a team, where different viewers care about different sections and a plain, well-labeled entry point saves everyone from hunting through unfamiliar tabs.

This guide covers building that first page from an empty canvas: placing a title, adding a placeholder visual, wiring up Power BI's built-in page navigator, and keeping the whole thing current without extra manual work.

steps.heading: Set up a dedicated landing page in your report
steps.body: Start from your Power BI report and add a new page specifically for this purpose. Name it something like "LANDING PAGE" so it's unmistakable in the page tab list, and drag it to the far left so it's the first thing anyone sees when the report opens. Keep this page visually separate from your working report pages; its job is orientation, not analysis, so resist the urge to cram a full chart onto it just because there's empty space available. Think of it as a table of contents, not another data page.

steps.heading: Add a visual placeholder to anchor the layout
steps.body: Drop a visual onto the canvas before you've decided exactly what data it will show. Power BI displays it as an empty gray placeholder reading "Select or drag fields to populate this visual," which is a normal, useful intermediate state and not something to worry about. Use it to block out the layout, deciding how much of the page a hero visual or summary chart should occupy relative to the surrounding whitespace, before committing to specific fields. Resize and reposition it a few times until the balance of the page feels right. It's faster to move an empty box around than to keep rebuilding a fully populated chart every time you want to try a different layout.

image.caption: An empty visual placeholder dropped onto the landing page canvas, used to block out the layout before any data fields are added.

steps.heading: Add a clear title to the page
steps.body: Place a text box or title element at the top of the page with your organization or dashboard name. Keep it short and immediately legible, since it's the first text a viewer reads before anything else on the page registers. Give it its own font weight or size so it reads as a page heading, not another chart label competing for attention. A one-line subtitle underneath, noting what the dashboard covers or how often it refreshes, adds useful context without turning the page into a wall of text.

image.caption: The landing page with a title added above the placeholder visual, giving the page a clear point of entry before any data is shown.

steps.heading: Insert a page navigator
steps.body: This is the part a lot of landing pages skip, then end up faking with a row of hand-built buttons. On the Insert tab, select Buttons > Navigator > Page navigator (in the Power BI service, it's the same path from the menu bar in edit mode). Power BI builds a row of buttons for you, one per report page, and keeps it in sync on its own: button labels match each page's display name, their order matches your page order, and both update automatically as you rename, add, or reorder pages. In Desktop or service edit mode, hold Ctrl and select a button to test where it navigates.

steps.heading: Control which pages the navigator shows
steps.body:
With the navigator selected, open the Format navigator pane and look under Pages, where you'll find toggles for showing hidden pages and showing tooltip pages, plus a Show list that lets you turn the button for any individual page on or off. Turn off the button for anything that's a work-in-progress or a tooltip-only helper page, so the navigator only exposes what's ready for viewers.

That Show list only controls the navigator's own buttons. It doesn't hide the underlying page. A page can still be reached by URL, by another navigator, or by a manually placed button even with its navigator entry turned off. To remove a page from the report's tab strip, right-click that page's tab and choose Hide instead.

image.caption: The Format navigator pane's Pages section, with Show toggles for the landing page and each individual report page, controlling what appears in the navigator.

steps.heading: Set up automated refresh so the page stays current
steps.body: A landing page loses credibility fast if the summary numbers on it go stale while the detail pages behind it stay current. A viewer who spots a stale headline number tends to distrust the rest of the report too, even if the deeper pages are perfectly up to date. Configure a scheduled refresh for the underlying dataset in the Power BI service, so the figures a viewer sees on first load are never more than a refresh cycle old. This matters more on a landing page than anywhere else in the report, since it's the number people remember even if they never click through to see anything else.

steps.heading: Design for the audience that only looks once
steps.body: Many viewers will open a dashboard, glance at the landing page, and leave without navigating further. Treat that as a design constraint, not a failure state to fight. Put the one or two numbers that matter most front and center, keep navigation obvious and sparse, and save deep drill-down detail for the pages behind the landing page instead of trying to fit everything onto the first screen. If you find yourself wanting to add a fifth or sixth summary tile, that's usually a sign it belongs on a dedicated overview page one click deeper, not on the landing page itself.

steps.heading: Add custom-labeled buttons when page names aren't enough
steps.body: The page navigator is the fastest path to working navigation, but its button text always matches a page's technical display name. When you want business-friendly labels instead, like "Sales Overview" instead of "Page 3," build individual buttons by hand: Insert > Buttons > Blank, then in the Format button pane turn Action on, set Type to Page navigation, and pick the destination page. Unlike the navigator, these buttons don't relabel themselves if you rename a page later, so budget a few minutes to check them after any page rename.

faq.question: What makes a good landing page for a Power BI dashboard?
faq.answer: A clear title, one or two headline metrics, and simple navigation to the pages behind it work better than trying to show every visual at once.

faq.question: Can I make my Power BI landing page update automatically?
faq.answer: Yes. Set up a scheduled refresh for the underlying dataset in the Power BI service, so the landing page's summary numbers stay current without manual intervention.

faq.question: How many visuals should I include on a landing page?
faq.answer: Fewer, well-chosen visuals generally work better than a crowded page. The goal is a quick overview and obvious navigation, not every possible detail.

faq.question: Do the page navigator's buttons update automatically when I rename or reorder pages?
faq.answer: Yes, that's what separates it from hand-built buttons. Labels, order, and the selected state all sync automatically as the report's pages change.

faq.question: How do I keep a work-in-progress page away from viewers?
faq.answer: Right-click that page's tab and choose Hide. Turning off its entry in a navigator's Show list only removes its button from that one navigator; the page itself stays reachable by URL or another button until it's hidden that way.

verifiedNote: Screens and layout choices come from a walkthrough recorded in July 2025. Re-checked against Microsoft's official Power BI documentation in September 2026, which showed the Format-pane page-visibility step this guide described only works after inserting a page navigator object (Insert > Buttons > Navigator > Page navigator) — a step the guide previously skipped — and that its Show toggles control a navigator's buttons, not the page's actual visibility, which is set separately via right-click > Hide.
